comparator.name: Dentistry (Tandheelkunde)
comparator.sourceNotes: The University of Groningen's current Dentistry documents page, rechecked on 14 October 2026 and last modified there on 21 September 2026, publishes the linked 2026-2027 Education and Examination Regulations (OER) as the governing bachelor regulation. Although the PDF's browser metadata title is 'concept', its running header identifies it throughout as the 2026-2027 Dentistry bachelor OER; the official documents page presents it as the current OER. Articles 3.6, 4.1 and 7.1 establish an ordinary three-year, 180-ECTS curriculum of 60 ECTS per year. All 29 listed components are compulsory and total 60+60+60=180 ECTS. Article 7.1 explicitly confirms that there are no tracks, no minor space and no electives, so the normalized generic Dentistry target has no route to select. The current programme page independently confirms a 36-month, 180-ECTS, Dutch-taught bachelor integrating biomedical, behavioural and dental science with extensive technical-skills training and patient care. Practical procedures are first trained on artificial jaws and teeth; diagnosis and treatment begin in Years 2 and 3; the curriculum culminates in the Bachelor Clinic and scientific work.

progressionAssessment.rationale: The schedule contains 24 unique courses, four per fixed semester, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and ten level-300 courses. Every formal prerequisite occurs earlier and every course is available in its assigned term. Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine precedes anatomy, cell biology, physiology, biochemistry, pharmacology, infection and immunity, disease mechanisms, laboratory work and molecular pathology; Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes cognition and psychology courses.

alternativeSelection.assessment: One complete related-fields programme passes the evidence, relevance and mechanical gates. It responds to the target's medical and scientific foundations, prevention, the relationship between bodily and oral health, patient behaviour and evidence-based practice through actual anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, cell biology, infection, immunity, pharmacology, pathology, epidemiology, health psychology, communication and research content. It is explicitly not presented as Dentistry or oral-health formation. A direct oral-science and clinical-dentistry direction cannot supply oral anatomy or biology, cariology, periodontology, dental materials, dental radiography, treatment planning, restorative procedures, preclinical simulation, manual dental skills or supervised patient care. No padded second programme is produced.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both establish healthy-human biomedical foundations; UCR covers cells, DNA, biochemistry and general health but not oral biology.
Both address normal human health and bodily function; UCR is a general physiology course and does not include dental health.
Both examine compromised health through biological mechanisms; UCR focuses general immunity and infection and does not teach oral disease.
Both examine mechanisms underlying compromised health; UCR provides general pathophysiology and clinical cases rather than dental diagnosis.
Both address maintaining health through prevention; UCR teaches epidemiology and population health rather than preventive dental care.
Both consider health behaviour and care in social context; UCR focuses psychological expertise and intervention in general medical settings.
Both include communication intended to influence health-related behaviour; UCR teaches general persuasion and framing rather than dental-patient consultation.
Both address development and behaviour across life stages; UCR is broad lifespan psychology rather than dental growth and development.
Both introduce scientific skills; UCR teaches general research design and statistics rather than dentistry-specific inquiry.
Both develop empirical and statistical methods; UCR focuses behavioural and health-science research.
Both culminate in evidence synthesis and advanced scientific work; UCR teaches systematic review and meta-analysis rather than independent dental research.
Both support professional and academic formation; UCR provides general ethical reflection, communication and independent-learning skills rather than dentist formation.

notes.text: The UCR programme combines human anatomy and physiology, biochemistry, cell biology, infection, immunity, pharmacology and disease mechanisms with epidemiology, health behaviour, communication and evidence synthesis. It does not reproduce oral anatomy or biology, oral disease science, dental materials and radiography, diagnosis and treatment planning, restorative procedures, preclinical technical skills, supervised patient care or dentist qualification.
